I'm thinking of building a playground for Next.js and Vercel. The docs are already good for both, and there's a playground for the app directory, but I want to build interactive, live examples of everything Next.js has to offer. The Vercel platform has a lot functionality that I would love to cover as well, as far as possible. I'm coming from the background of coaching web development in bootcamps and I know how difficult things are in the beginning. This playground serves the purpose of lowering the barrier to entry, but even for more experienced engineers it's a living guide.

The current landing page in the web project covers AI and misconceptions. There's a masterclass I held, as well. I've reconsidered since, and now I want to build the live playground using AI. Everything I build is public already (the repo is public on GitHub). The way I use Conductor with Claude Code under the hood I want to share as well using Entire.io.

For the first work in that direction, build the landing page. We need several working demos that show some aspect of Next.js and/or Vercel. Maybe you can figure out the most commonly used features or the ones that evoke looking them up in the docs a lot, so we can focus on them for the page. Keep the current design style. The current landing page is no longer needed; you can fully remove anything on it and its references, demos, everything. This is a fresh start. Keep the weekly digest form, though. I want to capture emails for people interested in more of what I do. I want to offer paid cohorts where I coach people.

It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. - vercel:deployment-expert: Specializes in Vercel deployment strategies, CI/CD pipelines, preview URLs, production promotions, rollbacks, environment variables, and domain configuration. Use when troubleshooting deployments, setting up CI/CD, or optimizing the deploy pipeline. (Tools: All tools)

- cancelling-queued-vercel-deployments: Use when queued Vercel deployments need to be cancelled by the GitHub author/login that triggered them — typically a CI bot like "actions-user" firing duplicate preview deployments, an Actions-minutes scare, or wanting a recurring sweeper to keep the queue clean while a noisy branch churns.
- deploy-to-vercel: Deploy applications and websites to Vercel. Use when the user requests deployment actions like "deploy my app", "deploy and give me the link", "push this live", or "create a preview deployment".
- effective-go: Apply Go best practices, idioms, and conventions from golang.org/doc/effective_go. Use when writing, reviewing, or refactoring Go code to ensure idiomatic, clean, and efficient implementations.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- get-api-docs: Use this skill when you need documentation for a third-party library, SDK, or API before writing code that uses it — for example, "use the OpenAI API", "call the Stripe API", "use the Anthropic SDK", "query Pinecone", or any time the user asks you to write code against an external service and you need current API reference. Fetch the docs with chub before answering, rather than relying on training knowledge.
- merging-branches-safely: Use when asked to merge or rebase one branch into another, or when resuming an in-progress merge/rebase with unresolved conflicts. Covers `git merge`, `git rebase`, and cleanup after conflict aborts. Do not use for cherry-pick, push, or PR creation.
- rebasing-renovate-prs-locally: Use when manually rebasing a Renovate PR for a pnpm monorepo locally, instead of waiting for the Renovate workflow. Triggers on draining a Renovate PR backlog, paused Renovate cron, slow CI lockfile regeneration, or "rebase this Renovate PR now without spending Actions minutes."
- sweep-vercel-queue: Two-pass sweep of a Vercel team's QUEUED deployments. Pass 1 cancels ALL queued PREVIEW deployments by a given githubLogin (e.g. a CI bot firing a preview per project on every push). Pass 2 cancels queued PRODUCTION deployments by a given githubLogin, keeping the newest per project so the latest code still ships. Use for "sweep the Vercel queue", "drain queued previews", "cancel a bot's preview deploys", "cancel stale prod deploys keep latest per app". Both passes are opt-in via env/config.
- vercel-cli-with-tokens: Deploy and manage projects on Vercel using token-based authentication. Use when working with Vercel CLI using access tokens rather than interactive login — e.g. "deploy to vercel", "set up vercel", "add environment variables to vercel".
- vercel-composition-patterns: React composition patterns that scale. Use when refactoring components with boolean prop proliferation, building flexible component libraries, or designing reusable APIs. Triggers on tasks involving compound components, render props, context providers, or component architecture. Includes React 19 API changes.
- vercel-optimize: Use for Vercel cost and performance optimization on deployed projects, especially Next.js, SvelteKit, Nuxt, and limited Astro apps. Collect Vercel metrics, usage, project config, and code scan results first; investigate only metric-backed candidates; produce ranked recommendations grounded in verified files and version-aware Vercel/framework docs. Trigger for Vercel bill reduction, slow or expensive routes, caching opportunities, Function Invocations, Build Minutes, Fast Data Transfer, Core Web Vitals, Bot Management, Fluid compute, or cost breakdown requests.

Triggers on tasks involving React components, Next.js pages, data fetching, bundle optimization, or performance improvements.

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f… [truncated]

## plugin:context7:context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

content.thinking:
I need to review the middleware setup to understand the i18n routing behavior and check how the design system handles font-display, then look at an existing demo component to see what interaction patterns are already established.

Before diving into the docs, I should first decide which demos to build—that'll determine what Next.js features I actually need to read about. The core question is what will resonate with bootcamp grads and junior developers.

The biggest pain points in Next.js are the ones people constantly look up: caching and revalidation (the infamous "why is my page stale?"), server vs client components and the conceptual confusion around hydration, streaming with Suspense to visualize progressive rendering, and server actions for form handling without traditional API routes. Auth gates and geolocation redirects via middleware, with a live demo showing the visitor's country pulled from Vercel's request headers—gracefully falling back on localhost. The caching headers like `x-vercel-cache: HIT/MISS` tie Next's caching strategy directly to Vercel's CDN, which is a nice way to show platform value without needing a full deployment.

For the actual demos, I'm thinking about constraints: the landing page needs to stay snappy with lazy-loaded or lightweight demo components, and everything has to be genuinely working code rather than mockups. A static shell with client islands calling real route handlers and server actions keeps the architecture clean. For streaming specifically, embedding an iframe of an actual streaming route would show true server streaming in action.

I'm torn between using an iframe (which is authentic and teaches Suspense/loading patterns, plus `loading="lazy"` means it only loads when scrolled into view) versus simulating streaming client-side. The iframe approach feels more honest to the playground's promise of real, live code. Though I'm also wondering if there's a way to stream the content directly into the page rather than through an iframe.

For the caching demo, I'm building a client component with three route handlers showing different cache strategies: one using `use cache` with ISR semantics, one fully dynamic with no-store, and one with tagged cache that can be revalidated via a server action. I'll display the server timestamps and cache headers to make the behavior visible.

I need to verify the Next 16 caching behavior first — particularly whether `use cache` works in route handlers and how the cacheComponents flag affects things. The cleanest approach for cached data fetching might be a server component or a route handler with the `revalidate` export, depending on what the docs confirm.

For the server actions demo, I'm thinking of a global counter or pin-board using useActionState with revalidation. The persistence question is tricky — I could use in-memory state (which would actually illustrate serverless statelessness nicely), but that might be confusing for a landing page. Better to use the database via Prisma if it's available as a dependency, though that means adding a counter table to the schema, which requires a cross-package change.

Actually, I'm realizing the web app already has @repo/database in its dependencies — probably for storing emails. Instead of adding a new counter model and running migrations, I could make the action do something more self-contained and genuinely useful: a server-side validation demo where you submit a word, the server validates and transforms it (timestamps it, checks length or content with zod), and returns the result via useActionState. That's stateless, real, and safe. The hook is powerful too — "It works with JavaScript turned off" — that's a strong teaching moment about progressive enhancement for beginners.

Or I could go with a cookie-based visitor counter: a server action that increments an httpOnly cookie, persisting the count across reloads without needing a database. The demo would be: form submission → server action increments the cookie → shows "You've pressed this button N times" with the count surviving page reloads. It's the same form-action pattern but with real persistence and personalization baked in. Both are solid, but the cookie approach combines the form-action demo with a tangible "remember me without a database" moment.

For dynamic OG images, I'm thinking of a live title input that generates a branded preview card server-side using ImageResponse from next/og. The user types a title, and the `/api/og` endpoint renders it as an image that updates in real-time—very visual and shareable, plus it showcases Vercel's edge-based image generation. Then for server vs client components, I want to move past just explaining the difference and actually show it: render two side-by-side components where one is server-only (displays server time and environment variables, no JavaScript shipped) and the other is client-side (interactive, shows bundle size). Let the user toggle between them to see the difference in action. The server card would actually show build-time rendering—the timestamp bakes in at build, and refreshing doesn't change it, which teaches static rendering as a real concept. The client card hydrates and handles interactivity. For routing, I'm thinking an interactive file-tree explorer that maps URLs to the layout and page chain—click a URL segment to see which files render, or type into the path. It's client-side and illustrative rather than a live server demo, but pairing it with an actual dynamic route would ground it in reality.

I could set up a catch-all route like `/playground/[...slug]` that echoes back whatever path you visit, with a link to try it live. That keeps it honest and working. Scoping down to five core demos instead of six feels right—each needs its own component, possibly a route, and clear copy. The foundation demos are server versus client rendering with static rendering truth, then streaming and suspense with a real streaming route in an iframe.

The remaining three would cover caching and revalidation with a tagged cache and revalidate button (the most-searched docs topic), server actions with cookies to show forms without API routes, and dynamic OG generation as a platform delight moment. I'd add a "coming next" section listing future demos like routing, middleware, next/image, fonts, parallel routes, and edge functions—signaling this is a living playground that grows. That ties perfectly to the weekly digest promise, where each Monday brings one new thing built.

For the page itself, I'm keeping the Contents navigation pattern from the original hero since it works well, then structuring each of the five demos with the same editorial rhythm: numbered, a hook, the interactive demo, and a meta-aside that reveals something. The "playground grows" section lists what's coming, the cohort section teases the paid bootcamp angle, the digest CTA reframes around weekly demos, and the FAQ addresses who this is for, whether it's free, and why live demos matter.

I'm renaming the wrapper component from MisconceptionWrapper to DemoSection — it'll handle the number, hook, question, and reveal pattern that gives the site its voice. See docs/01-app/02-guides/instant-navigation.mdx */} 15 16 > This page covers caching with [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), enabled by setting [`cacheComponents: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.ts` file. If you're not using Cache Components, see the [Caching and Revalidating (Previous Model)](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components) guide. 17 18 Caching is a technique for storing the result of data fetching and other computations so that future requests for the same data can be served faster, without doing the work again. 19 20 ## Enabling Cache Components 21 22 You can enable Cache Components by adding the [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) option to your Next config file: 23 24 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" highlight={4} switcher 25 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 26 27 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 28 cacheComponents: true, 29 } 30 31 export default nextConfig 32 ``` 33 34 ```js filename="next.config.js" highlight={3} switcher 35 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 36 const nextConfig = { 37 cacheComponents: true, 38 } 39 40 module.exports = nextConfig 41 ``` 42 43 > **Good to know:** When Cache Components is enabled, `GET` Route Handlers follow the same prerendering model as pages. See [Route Handlers with Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/route-handlers#with-cache-components) for details. 44 45 ## Usage 46 47 The [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive caches the return value of async functions and components. You can apply it at two levels: 48 49 - **Data-level**: Cache a function that fetches or computes data (e.g., `getProducts()`, `getUser(id)`) 50 - **UI-level**: Cache an entire component or page (e.g., `async function BlogPosts()`) 51 52 > Arguments and any closed-over values from parent scopes automatically become part of the [cache key](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache#cache-keys), which means different inputs will produce separate cache entries. This enables personalized or parameterized cached content. See [serialization requirements and constraints](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache#constraints) for details on what can be cached and how arguments work. 53 54 ### Data-level caching 55 56 To cache an asynchronous function that fetches data, add the `use cache` directive at the top of the function body: 57 58 ```tsx filename="app/lib/data.ts" highlight={3,4,5} 59 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 60 61 export async function getUsers() { 62 'use cache' 63 cacheLife('hours') 64 return db.query('SELECT * FROM users') 65 } 66 ``` 67 68 Data-level caching is useful when the same data is used across multiple components, or when you want to cache the data independently from the UI. 69 70 ### UI-level caching 71 72 To cache an entire component, page, or layout, add the `use cache` directive at the top of the component or page body: 73 74 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" highlight={1,4,5} 75 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 76 77 export default async function Page() { 78 'use cache' 79 cacheLife('hours') 80 81 const users = await db.query('SELECT * FROM users') 82 83 return ( 84
    85 {users.map((user) => ( 86
  • {user.name}
    • 87 ))} 88
89 ) 90 } 91 ``` 92 93 > If you add "`use cache`" at the top of a file, all exported functions in the file will be cached. 94 95 ### Streaming uncached data 96 97 For components that fetch data from an asynchronous source such as an API, a database, or any other async operation, and require fresh data on every request, do not use `"use cache"`. 98 99 Instead, wrap the component in [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense) and provide a fallback UI. At request time, React renders the fallback first, then streams in the resolved content once the async work completes. 100 101 ```tsx filename="page.tsx" 102 import { Suspense } from 'react' 103 104 async function LatestPosts() { 105 const data = await fetch('https://api.example.com/posts') 106 const posts = await data.json() 107 return ( 108
    109 {posts.map((post) => ( 110
  • {post.title}
    • 111 ))} 112
113 ) 114 } 115 116 export default function Page() { 117 return ( 118 <> 119

My Blog

120 Loading posts...

}> 121 122 123 124 ) 125 } 126 ``` 127 128 The fallback (`

Loading posts...

`) is included in the static shell, while the component's content streams in at request time. 129 130 `` provides a fallback UI while async work completes, but it does not itself opt a component into dynamic rendering. If a component only performs synchronous work, it will complete during prerendering regardless of whether it is wrapped in ``. 131 132 ## Working with runtime APIs 133 134 Runtime APIs require information that is only available when a user makes a request. These include: 135 136 - [`cookies`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies) - User's cookie data 137 - [`headers`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/headers) - Request headers 138 - [`searchParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#searchparams-optional) - URL query parameters 139 - [`params`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#params-optional) - Dynamic route parameters (unless at least one sample is provided via [`generateStaticParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params)). 140 141 Components that access runtime APIs should be wrapped in ``: 142 143 ```tsx filename="page.tsx" 144 import { cookies } from 'next/headers' 145 import { Suspense } from 'react' 146 147 async function UserGreeting() { 148 const cookieStore = await cookies() 149 const theme = cookieStore.get('theme')?.value || 'light' 150 return

Your theme: {theme}

151 } 152 153 export default function Page() { 154 return ( 155 <> 156

Dashboard

157 Loading...

}> 158 159 160 161 ) 162 } 163 ``` 164 165 ### Passing runtime values to cached functions 166 167 You can extract values from runtime APIs and pass them as arguments to cached functions: 168 169 ```tsx filename="app/profile/page.tsx" 170 import { cookies } from 'next/headers' 171 import { Suspense } from 'react' 172 173 export default function Page() { 174 return ( 175 Loading...}> 176 177 178 ) 179 } 180 181 // Component (not cached) reads runtime data 182 async function ProfileContent() { 183 const session = (await cookies()).get('session')?.value 184 return 185 } 186 187 // Cached component receives extracted value as a prop 188 async function CachedContent({ sessionId }: { sessionId: string }) { 189 'use cache' 190 // sessionId becomes part of the cache key 191 const data = await fetchUserData(sessionId) 192 return
{data}
193 } 194 ``` 195 196 At request time, `CachedContent` executes if no matching cache entry is found, and stores the result for future requests with the same `sessionId`. 197 198 By default, `use cache` stores entries [in-memory](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache#runtime-caching-considerations). In serverless environments where memory doesn't persist across requests, `CachedContent` may re-evaluate on every request. Consider [`'use cache: remote'`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote) for durable, shared caching. 199 200 ## Working with non-deterministic operations 201 202 Operations like `Math.random()`, `Date.now()`, or `crypto.randomUUID()` produce different values each time they execute. Cache Components requires you to explicitly handle these. 203 204 **To generate unique values per request**, defer to request time by calling [`connection()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/connection) before these operations, and wrap the component in ``: 205 206 ```tsx filename="page.tsx" 207 import { connection } from 'next/server' 208 import { Suspense } from 'react' 209 210 async function UniqueContent() { 211 await connection() 212 const uuid = crypto.randomUUID() 213 return

Request ID: {uuid}

214 } 215 216 export default function Page() { 217 return ( 218 Loading...

}> 219 220 221 ) 222 } 223 ``` 224 225 Alternatively, you can **cache the result** so all users see the same value until revalidation: 226 227 ```tsx filename="page.tsx" 228 export default async function Page() { 229 'use cache' 230 const buildId = crypto.randomUUID() 231 return

Build ID: {buildId}

232 } 233 ``` 234 235 ## Working with deterministic operations 236 237 Operations like synchronous I/O, module imports, and pure computations can complete during prerendering. Components using only these operations have their rendered output automatically included in the static HTML shell. 238 239 ```tsx filename="page.tsx" 240 import fs from 'node:fs' 241 242 export default async function Page() { 243 const content = fs.readFileSync('./config.json', 'utf-8') 244 const constants = await import('./constants.json') 245 const processed = JSON.parse(content).items.map((item) => item.value * 2) 246 247 return ( 248
249

{constants.appName}

250
    251 {processed.map((value, i) => ( 252
  • {value}
    • 253 ))} 254
255
256 ) 257 } 258 ``` 259 260 > **Good to know:** This includes queries to embedded databases with synchronous APIs, such as `better-sqlite3` or Node.js's built-in [`node:sqlite`](https://nodejs.org/api/sqlite.html). If you need per-request data from a synchronous source, call [`connection()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/connection) before the query. 261 262 ## How rendering works 263 264 At build time, Next.js renders your route's component tree. How each component is handled depends on the APIs it uses: 265 266 - [`use cache`](#usage): the result is cached and included in the static shell 267 - [``](#streaming-uncached-data): fallback UI is included in the static shell while the content streams at request time 268 - [Deterministic operations](#working-with-deterministic-operations): like pure computations and module imports are automatically included in the static shell 269 270 This generates a static shell consisting of HTML for initial page loads and a serialized [RSC Payload](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components#on-the-server) for client-side navigation, ensuring the browser receives fully rendered content instantly whether users navigate directly to the URL or transition from another page. 271 272 279 280 This rendering approach is called **Partial Prerendering (PPR)**, and it's the default behavior with Cache Components. 281 282 > You can verify that a route was fully prerendered by checking the [build output summary](/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next#next-build-options). Alternatively, see what content was added to the static shell of any page by viewing the page source in your browser. 283 284 291 292 Next.js requires you to explicitly handle components that can't complete during prerendering. If they aren't wrapped in `` or marked with `use cache`, you'll see an [`Uncached data was accessed outside of `](https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/blocking-route) error during development and build time. 293 294 > **🎥 Watch:** Why Partial Prerendering and how it works → [YouTube (10 minutes)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MTcPrTIBkpA). 295 296 ### Opting out of the static shell 297 298 Placing a `` boundary with an empty fallback above the document body in your Root Layout causes the entire app to defer to request time. Because the fallback is empty, there is no static shell to send immediately, so every request blocks until the page is fully rendered. To limit this to specific routes, use [multiple root layouts](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout#root-layout). 299 300 ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" highlight={1,10-12} 301 import { Suspense } from 'react' 302 303 export default function RootLayout({ 304 children, 305 }: { 306 children: React.ReactNode 307 }) { 308 return ( 309 310 311 {children} 312 313 314 ) 315 } 316 ``` 317 318 > **Good to know**: This same pattern applies when `generateViewport` accesses uncached dynamic data. See [Viewport with Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-viewport#with-cache-components) for a detailed example. 319 320 ### Putting it all together 321 322 Here's a complete example showing static content, cached dynamic content, and streaming dynamic content working together on a single page: 323 324 ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" 325 import { Suspense } from 'react' 326 import { cookies } from 'next/headers' 327 import { cacheLife, cacheTag, updateTag } from 'next/cache' 328 import Link from 'next/link' 329 330 export default function BlogPage() { 331 return ( 332 <> 333 {/* Static content - prerendered automatically */} 334
335

Our Blog

336
337 Home | About 338
339
340 341 {/* Cached dynamic content - included in the static shell */} 342 343 344 {/* Runtime dynamic content - streams at request time */} 345 Loading your preferences...

}> 346 347 348 349 {/* Mutation - server action that revalidates the cache */} 350 Loading...

}> 351 352 353 354 ) 355 } 356 357 // Everyone sees the same blog posts (revalidated every hour) 358 async function BlogPosts() { 359 'use cache' 360 cacheLife('hours') 361 cacheTag('posts') 362 363 const res = await fetch('https://api.vercel.app/blog') 364 const posts = await res.json() 365 366 return ( 367
368

Latest Posts

369
    370 {posts.slice(0, 5).map((post: any) => ( 371
  • 372

    {post.title}

    373

    374 By {post.author} on {post.date} 375

    376
    • 377 ))} 378
379
380 ) 381 } 382 383 // Personalized per user based on their cookie 384 async function UserPreferences() { 385 const theme = (await cookies()).get('theme')?.value || 'light' 386 const favoriteCategory = (await cookies()).get('category')?.value 387 388 return ( 389
390

Your theme: {theme}

391 {favoriteCategory &&

Favorite category: {favoriteCategory}

} 392
393 ) 394 } 395 396 // Admin-only form that creates a post and revalidates the cache 397 async function CreatePost() { 398 const isAdmin = (await cookies()).get('role')?.value === 'admin' 399 if (!isAdmin) return null 400 401 async function createPost(formData: FormData) { 402 'use server' 403 await db.post.create({ data: { title: formData.get('title') } }) 404 updateTag('posts') 405 } 406 407 return ( 408
409 410 411
412 ) 413 } 414 ``` 415 416 During prerendering, the header (static) and blog posts (cached with `use cache`) become part of the static shell along with the fallback UI for user preferences. Only the personalized preferences stream in at request time. When an admin publishes a new post, the [`updateTag`](/docs/app/getting-started/revalidating#updatetag) call immediately expires the blog posts cache so the next visitor sees it. 417 418 > **Good to know:** `generateMetadata` and `generateViewport` track runtime data access separately from the page. See [Metadata with Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#with-cache-components) and [Viewport with Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-viewport#with-cache-components) for how to handle this. 419

15	> This page covers revalidation with [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), enabled by setting [`cacheComponents: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.ts` file. If you're not using Cache Components, see the [Caching and Revalidating (Previous Model)](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components) guide.
16	
17	Revalidation is the process of updating cached data. It lets you keep serving fast, cached responses while ensuring content stays fresh. There are two strategies:
18	
19	- **Time-based revalidation**: Automatically refresh cached data after a set duration using [`cacheLife`](#cachelife).
20	- **On-demand revalidation**: Manually invalidate cached data after a mutation using [`revalidateTag`](#revalidatetag), [`updateTag`](#updatetag), or [`revalidatePath`](#revalidatepath).
21	
22	## `cacheLife`
23	
24	[`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) controls how long cached data remains valid. Use it inside a [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) scope to set the cache lifetime.
25	
26	```tsx filename="app/lib/data.ts" highlight={1,4,5}
27	import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache'
28	
29	export async function getProducts() {
30	  'use cache'
31	  cacheLife('hours')
32	  return db.query('SELECT * FROM products')
33	}
34	```
35	
36	`cacheLife` accepts a profile name or a custom configuration object:
37	
38	| Profile   | `stale` | `revalidate` | `expire` |
39	| --------- | ------- | ------------ | -------- |
40	| `default` | 5m      | 15m          | never    |
41	| `seconds` | 30s     | 1s           | 60s      |
42	| `minutes` | 5m      | 1m           | 1h       |
43	| `hours`   | 5m      | 1h           | 1d       |
44	| `days`    | 5m      | 1d           | 1w       |
45	| `weeks`   | 5m      | 1w           | 30d      |
46	| `max`     | 5m      | 30d          | 1y       |
47	
48	For fine-grained control, pass an object:
49	
50	```tsx highlight={2-6}
51	'use cache'
52	cacheLife({
53	  stale: 3600, // 1 hour until considered stale
54	  revalidate: 7200, // 2 hours until revalidated
55	  expire: 86400, // 1 day until expired
56	})
57	```
58	
59	> **Good to know:** A cache is considered "short-lived" when it uses the `seconds` profile, `revalidate: 0`, or `expire` under 5 minutes. Short-lived caches are automatically excluded from prerenders and become dynamic holes instead. See [Prerendering behavior](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#prerendering-behavior) for details.
60	
61	See the [`cacheLife` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) for all profiles and custom configuration options.
62	
63	## `cacheTag`
64	
65	[`cacheTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) lets you tag cached data so it can be invalidated on-demand. Use it inside a [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) scope:
66	
67	```tsx filename="app/lib/data.ts" switcher
68	import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'
69	
70	export async function getProducts() {
71	  'use cache'
72	  cacheTag('products')
73	  return db.query('SELECT * FROM products')
74	}
75	```
76	
77	```jsx filename="app/lib/data.js" switcher
78	import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'
79	
80	export async function getProducts() {
81	  'use cache'
82	  cacheTag('products')
83	  return db.query('SELECT * FROM products')
84	}
85	```
86	
87	Once tagged, invalidate the cache using [`revalidateTag`](#revalidatetag) or [`updateTag`](#updatetag).
88	
89	See the [`cacheTag` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) to learn more.
90	
91	## `revalidateTag`
92	
93	`revalidateTag` invalidates cache entries by tag using stale-while-revalidate semantics — stale content is served immediately while fresh content loads in the background. This is ideal for content where a slight delay in updates is acceptable, like blog posts or product catalogs.
94	
95	```tsx filename="app/lib/actions.ts" highlight={1,5} switcher
96	import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'
97	
98	export async function updateUser(id: string) {
99	  // Mutate data
100	  revalidateTag('user', 'max') // Recommended: stale-while-revalidate
101	}
102	```
103	
104	```jsx filename="app/lib/actions.js" highlight={1,5} switcher
105	import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'
106	
107	export async function updateUser(id) {
108	  // Mutate data
109	  revalidateTag('user', 'max') // Recommended: stale-while-revalidate
110	}
111	```
112	
113	You can reuse the same tag in multiple functions to revalidate them all at once. Call `revalidateTag` in a [Server Action](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data) or [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route).
114	
115	> **Good to know:** The second argument sets how long stale content can be served while fresh content generates in the background. Once it expires, subsequent requests block until fresh content is ready. Using `'max'` gives the longest stale window.
116	
117	See the [`revalidateTag` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) to learn more.
118	
119	## `updateTag`
120	
121	`updateTag` immediately expires cached data for read-your-own-writes scenarios — the user sees their change right away instead of stale content. Unlike `revalidateTag`, it can only be used in [Server Actions](/docs/app/guides/server-actions).
122	
123	```tsx filename="app/lib/actions.ts" highlight={1,12} switcher
124	import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'
125	import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'
126	
127	export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
128	  const post = await db.post.create({
129	    data: {
130	      title: formData.get('title'),
131	      content: formData.get('content'),
132	    },
133	  })
134	
135	  updateTag('posts')
136	  redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`)
137	}
138	```
139	
140	```jsx filename="app/lib/actions.js" highlight={1,12} switcher
141	import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'
142	import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'
143	
144	export async function createPost(formData) {
145	  const post = await db.post.create({
146	    data: {
147	      title: formData.get('title'),
148	      content: formData.get('content'),
149	    },
150	  })
151	
152	  updateTag('posts')
153	  redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`)
154	}
155	```
156	
157	|              | `updateTag`                                   | `revalidateTag`                      |
158	| ------------ | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
159	| **Where**    | Server Actions only                           | Server Actions and Route Handlers    |
160	| **Behavior** | Immediately expires cache                     | Stale-while-revalidate               |
161	| **Use case** | Read-your-own-writes (user sees their change) | Background refresh (slight delay OK) |
162	
163	See the [`updateTag` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag) to learn more.
164	
165	## `revalidatePath`
166	
167	`revalidatePath` invalidates all cached data for a specific route path. Use it when you want to revalidate a route without knowing which tags are associated with it.
168	
169	```tsx filename="app/lib/actions.ts" highlight={1,5} switcher
170	import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'
171	
172	export async function updateUser(id: string) {
173	  // Mutate data
174	  revalidatePath('/profile')
175	}
176	```
177	
178	```jsx filename="app/lib/actions.js" highlight={1,5} switcher
179	import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'
180	
181	export async function updateUser(id) {
182	  // Mutate data
183	  revalidatePath('/profile')
184	}
185	```
186	
187	> **Good to know**: Prefer tag-based revalidation (`revalidateTag`/`updateTag`) over path-based when possible — it's more precise and avoids over-invalidating.
188	
189	See the [`revalidatePath` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath) to learn more.
190	
191	## What should I cache?
192	
193	Cache data that doesn't depend on [runtime data](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#working-with-runtime-apis) and that you're OK serving from cache for a period of time. Use `use cache` with `cacheLife` to describe that behavior.
194	
195	For content management systems with update mechanisms, use tags with longer cache durations and rely on `revalidateTag` to refresh content when it actually changes, rather than expiring the cache preemptively.
196	
197	> **Good to know:** In serverless environments, in-memory cache entries may not persist across revalidations. See [runtime caching considerations](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache#runtime-caching-considerations) for details.

title: Revalidating
description: Learn how to revalidate cached data using time-based and on-demand strategies.
related:
  title: API Reference
  description: Learn more about the APIs mentioned on this page.
  links:
    - app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife
    - app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag
    - app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag
    - app/api-reference/functions/updateTag
    - app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath
---

> This page covers revalidation with [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), enabled by setting [`cacheComponents: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.ts` file. If you're not using Cache Components, see the [Caching and Revalidating (Previous Model)](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components) guide.

Revalidation is the process of updating cached data. It lets you keep serving fast, cached responses while ensuring content stays fresh. There are two strategies:

- **Time-based revalidation**: Automatically refresh cached data after a set duration using [`cacheLife`](#cachelife).
- **On-demand revalidation**: Manually invalidate cached data after a mutation using [`revalidateTag`](#revalidatetag), [`updateTag`](#updatetag), or [`revalidatePath`](#revalidatepath).

## `cacheLife`

[`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) controls how long cached data remains valid. Use it inside a [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) scope to set the cache lifetime.

```tsx filename="app/lib/data.ts" highlight={1,4,5}
import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache'

export async function getProducts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('hours')
  return db.query('SELECT * FROM products')
}
```

`cacheLife` accepts a profile name or a custom configuration object:

| Profile   | `stale` | `revalidate` | `expire` |
| --------- | ------- | ------------ | -------- |
| `default` | 5m      | 15m          | never    |
| `seconds` | 30s     | 1s           | 60s      |
| `minutes` | 5m      | 1m           | 1h       |
| `hours`   | 5m      | 1h           | 1d       |
| `days`    | 5m      | 1d           | 1w       |
| `weeks`   | 5m      | 1w           | 30d      |
| `max`     | 5m      | 30d          | 1y       |

For fine-grained control, pass an object:

```tsx highlight={2-6}
'use cache'
cacheLife({
  stale: 3600, // 1 hour until considered stale
  revalidate: 7200, // 2 hours until revalidated
  expire: 86400, // 1 day until expired
})
```

> **Good to know:** A cache is considered "short-lived" when it uses the `seconds` profile, `revalidate: 0`, or `expire` under 5 minutes. Short-lived caches are automatically excluded from prerenders and become dynamic holes instead. See [Prerendering behavior](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#prerendering-behavior) for details.

See the [`cacheLife` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) for all profiles and custom configuration options.

## `cacheTag`

[`cacheTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) lets you tag cached data so it can be invalidated on-demand. Use it inside a [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) scope:

```tsx filename="app/lib/data.ts" switcher
import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function getProducts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheTag('products')
  return db.query('SELECT * FROM products')
}
```

```jsx filename="app/lib/data.js" switcher
import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function getProducts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheTag('products')
  return db.query('SELECT * FROM products')
}
```

Once tagged, invalidate the cache using [`revalidateTag`](#revalidatetag) or [`updateTag`](#updatetag).

See the [`cacheTag` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) to learn more.

## `revalidateTag`

`revalidateTag` invalidates cache entries by tag using stale-while-revalidate semantics — stale content is served immediately while fresh content loads in the background. This is ideal for content where a slight delay in updates is acceptable, like blog posts or product catalogs.

```tsx filename="app/lib/actions.ts" highlight={1,5} switcher
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function updateUser(id: string) {
  // Mutate data
  revalidateTag('user', 'max') // Recommended: stale-while-revalidate
}
```

```jsx filename="app/lib/actions.js" highlight={1,5} switcher
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function updateUser(id) {
  // Mutate data
  revalidateTag('user', 'max') // Recommended: stale-while-revalidate
}
```

You can reuse the same tag in multiple functions to revalidate them all at once. Call `revalidateTag` in a [Server Action](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data) or [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route).

> **Good to know:** The second argument sets how long stale content can be served while fresh content generates in the background. Once it expires, subsequent requests block until fresh content is ready. Using `'max'` gives the longest stale window.

See the [`revalidateTag` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) to learn more.

## `updateTag`

`updateTag` immediately expires cached data for read-your-own-writes scenarios — the user sees their change right away instead of stale content. Unlike `revalidateTag`, it can only be used in [Server Actions](/docs/app/guides/server-actions).

```tsx filename="app/lib/actions.ts" highlight={1,12} switcher
import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'

export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  const post = await db.post.create({
    data: {
      title: formData.get('title'),
      content: formData.get('content'),
    },
  })

  updateTag('posts')
  redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`)
}
```

```jsx filename="app/lib/actions.js" highlight={1,12} switcher
import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'

export async function createPost(formData) {
  const post = await db.post.create({
    data: {
      title: formData.get('title'),
      content: formData.get('content'),
    },
  })

  updateTag('posts')
  redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`)
}
```

|              | `updateTag`                                   | `revalidateTag`                      |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| **Where**    | Server Actions only                           | Server Actions and Route Handlers    |
| **Behavior** | Immediately expires cache                     | Stale-while-revalidate               |
| **Use case** | Read-your-own-writes (user sees their change) | Background refresh (slight delay OK) |

See the [`updateTag` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag) to learn more.

## `revalidatePath`

`revalidatePath` invalidates all cached data for a specific route path. Use it when you want to revalidate a route without knowing which tags are associated with it.

```tsx filename="app/lib/actions.ts" highlight={1,5} switcher
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function updateUser(id: string) {
  // Mutate data
  revalidatePath('/profile')
```

> **Good to know**: Prefer tag-based revalidation (`revalidateTag`/`updateTag`) over path-based when possible — it's more precise and avoids over-invalidating.

See the [`revalidatePath` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath) to learn more.

## What should I cache?

Cache data that doesn't depend on [runtime data](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#working-with-runtime-apis) and that you're OK serving from cache for a period of time. Use `use cache` with `cacheLife` to describe that behavior.

For content management systems with update mechanisms, use tags with longer cache durations and rely on `revalidateTag` to refresh content when it actually changes, rather than expiring the cache preemptively.

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.

## Ground it in the subject

If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.

Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again

For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.

# Playground landing page — design (2026-07-31)

## Thesis
hasToggle.dev pivots to **the live playground for Next.js & Vercel**. The landing page
demonstrates itself: every demo is the real feature running on the page you're reading,
with real source shown. Built in public with AI (Conductor + Claude Code, shared via
Entire.io; repo public). Audience: bootcamp grads → seniors. Funnel: weekly digest
(kept form) + paid cohort teaser.

## Big technical decision
Enable `cacheComponents: true` (Next 16 Cache Components / PPR) for apps/web so the
page runs — and teaches — the current caching model (`use cache`, cacheLife, cacheTag,
updateTag, Suspense streaming). Requires `generateStaticParams` for `[locale]` and
determinism fixes (footer `new Date()`). Build is the gate; fallback is the previous
model if learn/masterclass routes break irreparably.

## Demos (syllabus order: before → during → after → beyond the request)
1. **The boundary** — server card (`use cache`, 0 kB JS, Node version + bake time) vs
   client card (`"use client"` counter). The mental model.
2. **The shell** — page's own bake timestamp via `use cache` + `cacheTag('landing-shell')`;
   "re-bake" button → server action → `updateTag`. Caching/revalidation, the #1 docs lookup.
3. **The stream** — Suspense hole with 3 staggered slow server rows (`connection()` + delay),
   re-run via `?stream=N` remount. PPR streaming, visible.
4. **The mutation** — server action increments an httpOnly cookie; count is read by a
   server component; setting the cookie re-renders. `useActionState` pending. Works with JS off.
5. **The image** — `/api/og` ImageResponse route; type a title, get a PNG. Also used as
   the page's real og:image.

## Signature element
Live mono "readouts" — every panel reports what the server actually did (baked at /
streamed at / cookie value / bytes). Hero carries the first one: shell bake time (static)
next to a streamed-in "now" (reserved height, no CLS).

## Removals
- `(demos)/` (plausibility, contract, mirror, completion, proof + wrapper), `misconceptions/`.
- Old hero/FAQ/Values/metadata copy (AI-misconceptions positioning).
- KEPT: digest form + confirm APIs, learn/* (incl. masterclass — unlinked now), blog,
  legal, contact, (counter) (used by learn/ref-vs-state), pricing (untouched boilerplate — flagged).

## Voice
Keep three layers: Surface (plain), Meta (Pratchett-dry `MetaAside`), Demo (the panels).
Numbers = syllabus order, stated as such. § dividers, plus-grid, Switzer/JetBrains Mono,
ht-cyan accents — all kept.

content.thinking:
The masterclass helper won't work for my needs since it's designed for animated editors with special token kinds. I need straightforward server-side rendering with Shiki v4, using `codeToHtml` with dual themes that match the existing CSS variables and light background styling. Setting up the themes as `github-light` and `github-dark` with `defaultColor: false` will emit the proper `--shiki-light` and `--shiki-dark` CSS variables.

For line numbering and displaying filenames, I can use a small transformer to inject the `title` attribute on the pre element, which the CSS will read via `.shiki[title]:before` to display the filename. Since the code strings are static module constants, I'll cache the `codeToHtml` function at build time with `use cache` and `cacheLife('max')` — the function takes serializable string arguments and returns HTML, so it fits the caching constraints. The main consideration is handling Shiki's WASM engine at build time; v4 supports a JavaScript RegExp engine option, though the default uses oniguruma WASM.

Now I'm planning the file structure: start with `next.config.ts` to enable `cacheComponents`, then set up `[locale]/layout.tsx` with `generateStaticParams` to handle localization, delete the old files, and build out the new shared components and page structure. I need to check where the locales list comes from — likely the internationalization package exports.

Designing the demo section component... Writing code display component... Writing component code... The bake ID gets displayed as a timestamp with a short suffix, and when the rebake action runs it calls updateTag to invalidate the cache, triggering a fresh render that the visitor sees immediately. The rebake button is a client component that triggers this server action, and since it's just invalidating one cached component per click, there's no need for rate limiting. The updateTag call works across instances on Vercel because it operates at the ISR/data-cache layer.

For the UI, I'm building a button that shows "re-baking…" while the action is pending, with copy that emphasizes the demo's point: this static shell was baked once and served many times, but now the visitor is about to re-bake it for everyone. The BakedPanel content is part of the static shell, so after updateTag triggers a re-render, the updated shell replaces it client-side.

Now moving into the streaming demo...

Each SlowRow component simulates a server-side delay, then returns a row with a label showing how long it took to arrive. I'm wrapping each row in its own Suspense boundary with a skeleton for progressive pop-in, nested inside the section's outer Suspense keyed by runId. For the rerun control, I'm using nuqs with `useQueryState("run", parseAsInteger)` and shallow: false to trigger a server fetch when the query param changes.

Now I'm setting up the page structure — when nuqs triggers a shallow: false update, it causes a server re-render. The page receives searchParams as a Promise and passes it down to StreamSection without awaiting it in the page body (that would error). StreamSection then awaits the promise to get the run ID and keys the rows accordingly, all wrapped in a Suspense boundary with a fallback.

On the initial load with run=0, rows stream in with staggered delays. When "Run it again" increments the run counter, the transition remounts the keyed boundaries, which forces the fallback to show since the key change creates a new mount. Each row displays its server-measured arrival offset, and there's a footer message about the shell being ready while the data cooked.

Now I'm moving into Demo 4 and setting up the server actions file...

Writing server action code... Writing OG image route... For the metadata, I'll skip setting metadataBase since Next 16 defaults it using the Vercel environment variables, and just construct the OG image URL with the encoded title and standard dimensions. Then I'm rewriting the hero section with a clearer lead statement and updating the asterisk note to emphasize that every demo is actually running live in production—no videos, no screenshots, just real features you can inspect.

The support text targets developers who learn hands-on, and the CTAs point to the first demo with a button labeled "Start poking" alongside a note confirming nothing's a mockup. For the readout signature, I'm creating a two-line mono display where the first line shows a static baked timestamp from a cache function, and the second line displays streamed content that updates after the server connection completes—with a fallback message that gets replaced by the actual timestamp once the stream arrives. The contents navigation stays intact with all five sections listed.

I'm swapping out the old values section entirely and replacing it with a roadmap showing upcoming demos as a checklist—routing, next/image, middleware, error handling, fonts, and more—with copy about adding one new exhibit weekly. Below that goes a "Built in the open" strip linking to the repo and crediting AI in the assembly.

Then comes a new cohort section before the digest, highlighting small paid bootcamp cohorts built on playground topics with early access through the mailing list. Finally, the digest CTA gets refreshed with copy about weekly demos landing Mondays, each with a write-up explaining what matters and where docs fall short.

For the FAQs, I'm reframing them around the playground as a hands-on complement to official docs — free forever, but with paid cohorts available. The questions cover who it's for (bootcamp grads through experienced devs), why it's different from just reading docs (it's the missing lab bench where you can experiment), and how it's built, which involves public development with AI.

The footer gets a line emphasizing that everything demonstrated is real and running live, plus a GitHub link in the sitemap. The metadata describes it as an interactive playground for Next.js and Vercel features, updated every Monday with new exhibits. I'm keeping the sitemap and robots untouched, along with the existing `/live` redirect.

For the routing, the `(playground)` route group doesn't need a page file since it's just organizational. I should verify that `global-error.tsx` doesn't import anything I'm removing, then run a typecheck to catch any broken imports after cleanup. The public assets like screenshots and testimonials are template leftovers—leaving those alone for now since they're out of scope.

Biome will handle formatting and prop sorting automatically when I run the fix command at the end. Time to start with the config and layout files, then handle the deletions.
